paragraphs: Sometimes the parts that make up the State cannot be held in exact proportion, or causes that cannot be removed keep shifting how one part stands toward another. The remedy then is a special magistracy that does not merge into the body of the State. It puts each term back in its right relation to the others, and it serves as a link, a middle term, between prince and people, or between prince and Sovereign, or, where necessary, between both at once.

This body I shall call the _tribunate_. It guards the laws and the legislative power. At times it shields the Sovereign from the government, as the tribunes of the people did at Rome. At times it backs the government against the people, as the Council of Ten does today at Venice. And at times it keeps the two in balance, as the Ephors did at Sparta.

The tribunate is not a constituent part of the city, and it should hold no share of legislative or executive power. Yet that is exactly what makes its power greater: it can do nothing, but it can stop anything from being done. As defender of the laws it is more sacred and more revered than the prince who carries them out or the Sovereign who enacts them. Rome showed this plainly, when the proud patricians, who despised the people, had to bow before one of its officers, a man with neither auspices nor jurisdiction.

A tribunate that is wisely tempered is the firmest support a good constitution can have. But if its strength goes even slightly too far, it throws the whole State into disorder. Weakness, by contrast, is not in its nature: so long as it is anything at all, it is never less than it ought to be.

It slides into tyranny when it seizes the executive power, which it ought only to restrain, and when it tries to do without the laws, which it ought only to protect. The immense power of the Ephors did no harm while Sparta kept its morals, but once corruption had set in, that power sped it along. Agis was slaughtered by these tyrants, and his successor Cleomenes avenged his blood. The Ephors’ crime and their punishment both hastened the ruin of the republic, and after Cleomenes Sparta counted for nothing. Rome fell the same way. The tribunes grabbed more and more power, bit by bit, and in the end that power, together with laws made to secure liberty, shielded the emperors who destroyed it. As for the Venetian Council of Ten, it is a tribunal of blood, dreaded by patricians and people alike. It no longer offers the laws any lofty protection, now that they have been degraded. It simply strikes in the dark, and no one dares to take note of the blows.

Like the government, the tribunate grows weaker as the number of its members increases. The tribunes of the Roman people, who at first numbered only two and then five, wished to double that number. The senate let them, confident that it could use one tribune to check another, as indeed it later did freely.

The best way to prevent usurpations by so formidable a body would be not to make it permanent, but to regulate the periods during which it stays in abeyance, though no government has yet used this method. These intervals should not be long enough to give abuses time to grow strong. They may be fixed by law in such a way that they can easily be shortened, when necessary, by extraordinary commissions.

I see no drawback in this method. As I have said, the tribunate is no part of the constitution, so removing it leaves the constitution untouched. The method also seems effective, because a magistrate who has just been restored begins with the power the law gives him, not the power his predecessor wielded.
